title: Equivalence principle and the principles of general relativity
scope: The physical argument that gravity is spacetime geometry and the principles that turn it into a theory: Mach's principle and Newton's bucket; inertial versus gravitational mass and the universality of free fall with its torsion-balance tests; the weak, Einstein and strong equivalence principles (with the books' conflicting names) and the Einstein lift; free fall, weight, freely falling and local inertial frames as physics; tides as the only local signature of gravity and the resulting absence of global inertial frames; gravitational redshift and time dilation with their clock experiments (Pound-Rebka, Gravity Probe A, Hafele-Keating, GPS) and Schild's argument; general relativity and general covariance; the comma-to-semicolon rule and minimal versus non-minimal coupling; the correspondence principle, weak-field limit, weak-field metric and Newtonian limit of geodesic motion; metric theories and why scalar theories fail. The local-flatness theorem as mathematics, geodesic deviation, exact Schwarzschild redshift and the Newtonian limit of the field equations live in other domains.

concepts.title: Heuristic role of physical principles
concepts.summary: General relativity was built by letting a handful of physical principles (Mach, equivalence, covariance, minimal coupling, correspondence) constrain the mathematics. They are imprecise, but they explain why the theory has its form and where to look if it must be changed.

concepts.title: Newtonian spacetime
aliases: Newtonian spacetime as a bundle over time
concepts.summary: Newton's arena is a stack of Euclidean spaces, one per instant of absolute time, related by Galilean transformations. Observers agree on time intervals and on distances between simultaneous events, but there is no single invariant spacetime length; relativity replaces this layered structure with one metric.

names: Newtonian spacetime as a bundle over time

merged_from: Newtonian spacetime as a bundle over time

concepts.title: Newton's bucket experiment
concepts.summary: A bucket of water set spinning shows a curved surface only when the water itself rotates, regardless of its motion relative to the bucket. Newton read this as evidence for rotation relative to absolute space; Mach asked whether the distant matter of the universe is the real reference.

concepts.title: Mach's principle
concepts.summary: The idea that inertia and the inertial frames are fixed by the distribution of all matter in the universe rather than by absolute space. It inspired Einstein, and GR realizes it only partially: matter shapes geometry, yet vacuum solutions such as Minkowski space still have inertia.

names: Inertial frames non-rotating relative to the distant stars

merged_from: Inertial frames non-rotating relative to the distant stars
concepts.notes: Folds in DIV's pendulum-at-the-pole coincidence (local inertial frames do not rotate relative to the distant stars) as supporting evidence, and DIV's Machian prediction that inertia would be anisotropic in a lumpy universe. DIV states three sharpened forms M1-M3. Frame dragging as a partial Machian effect belongs with rotating spacetimes.

concepts.title: Hughes-Drever experiment
concepts.summary: Nuclear magnetic resonance experiments around 1960 that looked for a direction dependence of inertial mass as the Earth turned relative to the galaxy and found none to extraordinary precision. The null result rules out the anisotropic inertia a naive Machian picture predicts and is now read as a test of local Lorentz invariance.

concepts.title: Free fall
concepts.summary: A body is in free fall when gravity is the only influence on it and no non-gravitational force acts. A freely falling observer feels no weight and an accelerometer she carries reads zero.

names: free fall as zero proper acceleration

concepts.title: Universality of free fall
concepts.summary: All test bodies started from the same place with the same velocity follow the same trajectory in a gravitational field, whatever their mass or composition. Newton treated this as a coincidence; general relativity makes it the reason gravity can be geometry.
concepts.notes: Naming alert: DIV ch09 calls this P1 the 'strong' form while its own ch16 and modern usage call it the weak equivalence principle. Unlike electromagnetism, no particle is immune to gravity, so no free particle can mark a non-falling inertial frame.

concepts.title: Equality of inertial and gravitational mass
aliases: equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass
equality of inertial and passive gravitational mass
concepts.summary: The mass that resists acceleration equals the mass that couples to a gravitational field, for every body. Cancelling the two in Newton's second law shows why free-fall acceleration is independent of the body, which is the universality of free fall in Newtonian language.

names: equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass
Equality of inertial and passive gravitational mass

merged_from: Equality of inertial and passive gravitational mass
equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass

concepts.title: Equality of active and passive gravitational mass
concepts.summary: A body's strength as a source of gravity equals its response to gravity. In Newtonian theory this follows from the third law applied to two bodies attracting each other, and it guarantees momentum conservation for gravitating systems.

names: Equality of passive and active gravitational mass

merged_from: Equality of passive and active gravitational mass

concepts.title: Eotvos experiment
aliases: tests of the weak equivalence principle
concepts.summary: A torsion balance carrying two different materials twists if their ratios of gravitational to inertial mass differ. Such experiments, and their satellite successors, bound the fractional difference in free-fall acceleration (the Eotvos ratio) to parts in 10^13 and better.

names: tests of the weak equivalence principle

merged_from: tests of the weak equivalence principle
concepts.notes: The Eotvos ratio eta = 2|a1 - a2|/|a1 + a2| is folded in as the figure of merit. History runs from Eotvos through Dicke and Braginsky to space tests.

concepts.title: Universal coupling of gravity
concepts.summary: Gravity acts on and is sourced by everything: all matter and, through mass-energy equivalence, all forms of energy. Nothing can be shielded from it, which is why every contribution to the stress-energy must gravitate.
concepts.notes: DIV ch09 labels this P2 the 'weak' principle of equivalence, which clashes with modern naming; avoid that label with learners.

concepts.title: Equivalence of gravity and acceleration
aliases: uniform acceleration equivalent to a uniform gravitational field
concepts.summary: In a small enough region, a frame accelerating uniformly relative to an inertial frame cannot be distinguished by any local experiment from a frame held at rest in a uniform gravitational field. A strictly uniform field can therefore be transformed away entirely and has no invariant content.
concepts.notes: GA ch06 uses the equivalence to show that light bends in an accelerating rocket and hence in a gravitational field. The standard misconception is that gravity is only a choice of frame everywhere; real fields are non-uniform and their tides remain.

concepts.title: Gravity as an inertial force
concepts.summary: Of all forces, only inertial (fictitious) forces and gravity are proportional to the mass of the body acted on. Einstein read this as a common origin: gravity is an inertial effect of describing motion from frames that are not freely falling, which in geometric language puts gravity into the connection coefficients.

concepts.title: Weak equivalence principle
concepts.summary: The motion of an uncharged test body under gravity alone depends only on its initial position and velocity, so a freely falling frame removes gravitational acceleration for all nearby particles at once. In geometric form it says free test particles follow timelike geodesics of one spacetime metric.
concepts.notes: 'Weak' because it concerns only mechanical, gravitational motion of test bodies. SCH ch07 turns it into the postulate that free particles follow geodesics. It is among the best-tested statements in physics. Schutz states the geodesic form of this principle as a geodesic postulate; see geodesic-postulate.

concepts.title: Freely falling frame
aliases: co-moving frame of a test particle
concepts.summary: A reference frame that moves with a test particle falling under gravity alone. If it also does not rotate, gravity disappears inside it over a small region, and it stays locally inertial along the whole free-fall world line.
concepts.notes: Einstein's 'happiest thought' of a person falling from a roof supplies the image. GA distinguishes it from a general local inertial frame defined at a single event.

concepts.title: Einstein lift thought experiment
concepts.summary: An observer in a sealed room compares four cases: an accelerating rocket, a coasting rocket, resting on Earth, and falling freely. With one released body the pairs (accelerating, resting) and (coasting, falling) look identical; with two separated bodies, relative motion reveals the real field.
concepts.notes: DIV ch09 gives the local version; DIV ch10 repeats the four cases with two balls to expose tides, folded in here. Legacy 'three cabins' comparison is the same idea.

concepts.title: Tidal force
concepts.summary: Tidal effects are relative accelerations of nearby freely falling bodies, caused by the spatial variation of the gravitational field. No choice of frame removes them, so they are the local, frame-independent signature of real gravity, which general relativity identifies with spacetime curvature.

names: tidal effects as the measurable signature of gravity
Tidal relative acceleration as the signature of gravitation
free fall does not remove all gravity

merged_from: tidal effects as the measurable signature of gravity
Tidal relative acceleration as the signature of gravitation
concepts.notes: A falling cloud of test particles stretches along the direction to the mass and squeezes across it. One particle or one accelerometer cannot distinguish gravity from acceleration or from bad coordinates; two separated particles can. The quantitative version (Riemann tensor via geodesic deviation) lives in curvature.

concepts.title: Local inertial frame
concepts.summary: A freely falling, non-rotating frame in which special relativity holds within a region small enough that tidal variations are undetectable. Mathematically, coordinates at an event where the metric is Minkowskian and its first derivatives vanish, so the Christoffel symbols are zero there.

names: separation of local physics from cosmology

merged_from: separation of local physics from cosmology
concepts.notes: Its existence at every event is the physics; the proof by counting Taylor coefficients belongs to manifolds-and-metrics (local-flatness-theorem). GA's 'local Lorentz frame' is the orthonormal version an observer uses to read measured components. SCH ch13 draws a consequence: because spacetime is locally flat, local physics (stars, labs) needs no knowledge of cosmology.

concepts.title: Einstein equivalence principle
concepts.summary: In any freely falling local inertial frame, every local non-gravitational experiment gives the same result as in special relativity. It combines the weak equivalence principle with local Lorentz invariance and local position invariance, and it implies that gravity is described by a spacetime metric.
concepts.notes: Naming alert: GA ch06 calls this the 'strong equivalence principle'; modern usage reserves 'strong' for a version including gravitational experiments. Consequence: gravity has no locally detectable effect, and its influence appears only in comparisons across finite regions. Gifted Amateur calls this principle the strong equivalence principle; that name is reserved here for strong-equivalence-principle.

concepts.title: Local Lorentz invariance
concepts.summary: The outcome of a small non-gravitational experiment in a freely falling laboratory does not depend on the velocity of that laboratory. It is one of the three clauses of the Einstein equivalence principle and is tested by modern Michelson-Morley-type and clock-comparison experiments.

concepts.title: Local position invariance
concepts.summary: The outcome of a small non-gravitational experiment in a freely falling laboratory does not depend on where or when it is done, so dimensionless constants of nature are the same everywhere and always. Redshift experiments with clocks test its spatial part.

concepts.title: Strong equivalence principle
concepts.summary: The extension of the Einstein equivalence principle to all experiments, including gravitational ones and self-gravitating bodies: local physics in free fall, gravity included, is independent of velocity, location and gravitational binding energy. General relativity satisfies it; many alternative theories do not, which lunar laser ranging tests.
concepts.notes: None of the three books teaches the modern version. GA ch06 uses the name for what is now called the Einstein equivalence principle, and DIV ch09 attaches 'strong' to universality of free fall. The tutor should present the three-level ladder WEP, EEP, SEP and flag both book usages. Kept as a concept so tests such as the Nordtvedt effect have an anchor.

concepts.title: Weightlessness and weight as a contact force
aliases: weight as a non-gravitational contact force
proper acceleration reading of an accelerometer
concepts.summary: What we feel as weight is not gravity but the floor pushing us off our free-fall path; a scale measures that support force. Astronauts in orbit feel weightless even though gravity there is nearly as strong as at the surface, because they are falling freely.

names: weight as a non-gravitational contact force

merged_from: weight as a non-gravitational contact force
concepts.notes: Legacy course opens with a falling scale and an accelerometer; weightlessness does not mean no tides.

concepts.title: Gravitational redshift
concepts.summary: Light climbing out of a gravitational potential arrives with lower frequency; to first order the fractional shift is gh/c^2, or the potential difference over c^2. It follows from energy conservation or from the equivalence principle alone, before any field equations.

names: gravitational redshift from quantum time evolution

merged_from: gravitational redshift from quantum time evolution
concepts.notes: Examples folded in: SCH's tower of falling mass converted to a photon (no perpetual motion), the Doppler reading from a freely falling frame, DIV's static-observer derivation for any static metric, the fractional frequency shift, and Coleman's quantum argument (GA ch49). Exact Schwarzschild and stellar-surface versions belong to schwarzschild-geometry-and-stars; cosmological redshift to cosmological-kinematics.

concepts.title: Gravitational time dilation
aliases: clocks run slow in a potential well
concepts.summary: A clock held lower in a gravitational potential ticks more slowly, when compared by signals, than an identical clock higher up; in a weak field the rate ratio is about 1 + (difference in potential)/c^2. It is the clock-rate face of gravitational redshift and needs no curvature: accelerated clocks in flat spacetime show it too.
concepts.notes: GA ch06 derives it from g_00 of the weak-field metric and by dropping a clock from far away; the legacy course derives the rate 1 + az/c^2 for a rigid accelerated array. The Schwarzschild static-clock factor belongs to schwarzschild-geometry-and-stars.

concepts.title: Pound-Rebka experiment
concepts.summary: In 1960 (improved with Snider in 1965) gamma rays were sent up a 22.5 m tower at Harvard, using the Mossbauer effect to resolve frequency shifts of a few parts in 10^15. A small Doppler velocity of the source compensated the gravitational shift and confirmed the predicted gh/c^2 to about 1 percent.

concepts.title: Gravity Probe A
concepts.summary: A 1976 rocket flight carried a hydrogen-maser clock to about 10,000 km and compared it with a ground maser, confirming the gravitational frequency shift to a few parts in 10^4, about a hundred times better than the tower experiment.

names: Gravity Probe A rocket redshift test

merged_from: Gravity Probe A rocket redshift test

concepts.title: Hafele-Keating experiment
concepts.summary: Atomic clocks flown around the world in both directions were compared with ground clocks; the measured gains and losses matched the combination of velocity time dilation and gravitational time dilation at altitude.
concepts.notes: DIV ch03 cites it without names as evidence for time dilation.

concepts.title: GPS relativistic corrections
concepts.summary: GPS satellite clocks run slow by about 7 microseconds per day from their orbital speed and fast by about 45 from their altitude, a net gain near 38 microseconds per day. Left uncorrected, this would build up positioning errors of kilometres per day.
concepts.notes: For circular orbits the net rate relative to a surface clock changes sign at an altitude of half an Earth radius (legacy figure and lab).

concepts.title: Schild's redshift argument
aliases: nonexistence of a Lorentz frame at rest on Earth
concepts.summary: If gravitational redshift occurs in a static field, a frame at rest on Earth cannot have Minkowski geometry: static time translation would force equal intervals between successive light crests at the bottom and top of a tower, contradicting the measured frequency difference. Gravity therefore requires curved spacetime.

names: nonexistence of a Lorentz frame at rest on Earth

merged_from: nonexistence of a Lorentz frame at rest on Earth

concepts.title: Absence of global inertial frames
aliases: no global inertial frames in a gravitational field
gravity as the obstacle to global inertial frames
concepts.summary: When gravity is present one generally cannot build a single frame with rigid rulers, synchronized clocks and Euclidean geometry everywhere: freely falling frames are inertial only locally, and non-uniform fields prevent patching them together. This is the reason special relativity must be generalized.

names: gravity as the obstacle to global inertial frames

merged_from: gravity as the obstacle to global inertial frames

concepts.title: Gravity as spacetime curvature
aliases: curved spacetime from the equivalence principle
concepts.summary: Since gravity enters motion like an inertial effect yet real fields cannot be removed globally, gravity is modelled as the curvature of spacetime: matter tells spacetime how to curve, and spacetime tells free bodies how to move. The connection stays the metric connection, but the metric is no longer flat.

names: Curved space-time from the equivalence principle

merged_from: Curved space-time from the equivalence principle

concepts.title: Metric as gravitational potential
concepts.summary: Connection coefficients play the role of gravitational forces and are first derivatives of the metric, so the metric components take over the role of the Newtonian potential. Hence the field equations should be second-order differential equations for the metric, as Poisson is for the potential.

concepts.title: Rubber-sheet analogy
concepts.summary: The popular picture of a heavy ball denting a stretched sheet so that marbles roll on curved paths. It hints at geodesic motion but is circular (it uses gravity to pull the ball down) and shows only spatial curvature, missing the time part of the metric that governs slow-moving bodies.

concepts.title: Principle of general relativity
concepts.summary: All observers, inertial or not, are equally able to discover the laws of physics. It extends the special principle of relativity, although the essential difference between the two theories is the inclusion of gravity, not the admission of accelerated observers.
concepts.notes: SCH ch01 stresses that the name 'general' is misleading: special relativity already handles accelerated observers, and the real distinction is gravity.

concepts.title: General covariance
concepts.summary: Physical laws must be expressible as tensor equations that hold in every coordinate system, since curved spacetime has no privileged coordinates. On its own it has little content, because almost any theory can be written covariantly; its force comes when paired with the equivalence principle.
concepts.notes: DIV caveats: symmetry-adapted coordinates are still useful, and covariance alone does not restrict a theory (Kretschmann). GA illustrates a non-covariant law that singles out one component. The hole argument belongs to einstein-field-equations.

concepts.title: Correspondence principle
aliases: recovery of the old theory in its domain
concepts.summary: A new theory must reproduce the confirmed predictions of the theory it replaces within that theory's domain. General relativity must reduce to special relativity without gravity and to Newtonian gravity for weak fields, slow motion and small pressures.

concepts.title: Weak-field limit
concepts.summary: A gravitational field is weak when coordinates exist in which the metric differs from Minkowski by small perturbations, g = eta + h with |h| << 1, equivalently when |Phi|/c^2 << 1. Terms of second order in the perturbation or potential are then dropped.
concepts.notes: The ratio |Phi|/c^2 (about 10^-9 at Earth's surface, near 0.2 for neutron stars) measures how relativistic a field is. Gauge freedom of the perturbation belongs to gravitational-waves.

concepts.title: Newtonian limit
concepts.summary: The regime of weak fields, speeds small compared with light, and stresses small compared with energy density, in which general relativity must reduce to Newtonian gravity. For slow bodies the time component of the four-velocity dominates, and slowness itself forces the field to be weak.
concepts.notes: Carrying out the limit on the field equations to fix 8 pi G belongs to einstein-field-equations.

concepts.title: Weak-field metric
concepts.summary: The first-order metric of a static weak field with Newtonian potential Phi is ds^2 = -(1 + 2Phi/c^2)c^2 dt^2 + (1 - 2Phi/c^2)(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2). The time part alone reproduces Newtonian motion and clock-rate effects; the equal spatial part matters for light.

names: weak-field metric with spatial curvature term
weak-field metric with Phi and Psi

merged_from: weak-field metric with spatial curvature term
concepts.notes: Books quote it early (SCH ch07, GA ch05) and derive it later from the linearized field equations (SCH ch08, GA ch14, GA ch45). GA ch02 motivates g_00 by matching the free-particle action with a potential. Signs depend on signature: DIV writes g_00 = 1 + 2phi/c^2.

concepts.title: Newtonian limit of the geodesic equation
aliases: recovery of Newton's second law from geodesics
concepts.summary: For slow motion in the weak-field metric, only Gamma^i_00 = partial_i Phi survives, and the geodesic equation reduces to d^2x^i/dt^2 = -partial_i Phi, Newton's law of gravity. Read backwards, requiring Newtonian motion fixes g_00 = -(1 + 2Phi/c^2) without any field equation.

names: Christoffel symbols of the weak-field metric
Newtonian limit of the geodesic equation

merged_from: Newtonian limit of the geodesic equation
Christoffel symbols of the weak-field metric
concepts.notes: The time component gives energy conservation in a static field. The Christoffel symbols of the weak-field metric are the worked example (owned by connection-and-parallel-transport).

concepts.title: Newtonian gravity as curvature of time
concepts.summary: For slowly moving bodies the proper time along a world line is dominated by the g_00 term, so Newtonian orbits are set by g_00 alone, the same component that fixes gravitational redshift. Spatial curvature only shows up in post-Newtonian effects such as the full bending of light.

names: Newtonian gravity as curvature of time

merged_from: Newtonian gravity as curvature of time
concepts.notes: SCH ch11 uses it to explain the factor of two in light deflection.

concepts.title: Spatial metric of a stationary spacetime
aliases: radar distance in a stationary spacetime
concepts.summary: In a stationary metric with time-space cross terms, the distance measured by bouncing light between neighbouring points is dl^2 = (g_ij - g_0i g_0j / g_00) dx^i dx^j. It is how rulers, rather than coordinates, define lengths for observers at rest in the field.

names: spatial metric of a stationary spacetime

merged_from: spatial metric of a stationary spacetime
concepts.notes: GA ch06 exercise; the same set of exercises leads to clock synchronization in rotating frames and the Sagnac effect.

concepts.title: Metric theory of gravity
concepts.summary: A theory in which spacetime carries a symmetric metric, freely falling test bodies follow its geodesics, and non-gravitational laws take special-relativistic form in local freely falling frames. The Einstein equivalence principle essentially forces this structure; GR and Brans-Dicke are both metric theories.
concepts.notes: DIV ch16 gives Will's plausibility argument (Schiff conjecture territory) and uses the class to compare rivals through PPN parameters.

concepts.title: Comma-goes-to-semicolon rule
concepts.summary: To carry a law from special to general relativity, write it as a tensor equation, then replace eta by g and partial derivatives (commas) by covariant derivatives (semicolons). It works because the law holds in a local inertial frame, where the two derivatives agree, and a tensor equation true in one frame is true in all.

names: minimal coupling via eta to g replacement

merged_from: minimal coupling via eta to g replacement
concepts.notes: Standard examples: T^{mu nu}_{;nu} = 0 for fluids, (n U^alpha)_{;alpha} = 0, Maxwell equations, the force law. GA ch33 notes a case where commas and semicolons agree because Christoffel terms cancel.

concepts.title: Minimal coupling
concepts.summary: When a special-relativistic law or Lagrangian is moved into curved spacetime, add no terms that involve curvature explicitly: replace eta by g, partial by covariant derivatives, and d^4x by sqrt(-g) d^4x, and stop. It is a simplicity rule, not a consequence of the equivalence principle.
concepts.notes: DIV presents it as Occam's razor and admits it is vague. GA ch40 and DIV ch11 apply it to field Lagrangians (scalar field); the action machinery belongs to action-principles-and-field-theory.

concepts.title: Non-minimal coupling
concepts.summary: Terms such as a Ricci-scalar coupling xi R phi^2 that vanish in flat spacetime, so agreement with special relativity cannot rule them out. They also arise as an ambiguity: covariant derivatives do not commute, so a flat law with second derivatives has several curved versions differing by curvature terms.

names: minimal coupling is not unique (xi R phi^2)

concepts.notes: SCH ch07 illustrates with a rival conservation law (nU^alpha)_{;alpha} = q R^2; GA ch35 with a Maxwell-like equation for A^mu.

concepts.title: Scalar theory of gravity
concepts.summary: Attempts to describe gravity by a single scalar potential on flat spacetime, or equivalently a conformally flat metric. They can respect the weak equivalence principle but couple only to the trace of the stress-energy, so light (traceless) is not deflected, contradicting observation.
concepts.notes: Appears in GA exercises (ch20 flat-space scalar theory after Thorne and Blandford, ch42 conformally flat trial theory, ch47 spin-0 mediator). Modern scalar-tensor theories belong to quantum-gravity-and-beyond.
